sents: I am not an expert on why dry-stone walls fail, and people who have studied it properly would know better than I do.
In my second year as a waller I built forty metres along the top of a hill farm.
After one wet winter a stretch of it bellied out like a full sack.
I rebuilt the stretch with heavier face stones, and the next spring it bellied again.
An older waller who was passing pulled a single face stone out of it and put his arm into the wall up to the elbow.
There was nothing behind the stone.

Thinking about that hollow afterwards, I started to wonder whether the middle of a wall might matter more than its faces, and the interesting thing I found is that a wall seems to fail from the inside.
Suppose the small stones in the middle, which I believe is called the hearting, are thrown in loose.
They would presumably settle, and the faces might then have nothing to lean on.
From what I have read since, each stone should probably be placed and wedged by hand, and I gather that a long stone is meant to run through the wall every metre or so.
I have built that way for twenty years, and so far none of those walls has moved, though I could not say for certain why.

[P3] Suppose the small stones in the middle, which I believe is called the hearting, are thrown in loose. They would presumably settle, and the faces might then have nothing to lean on. Score each sentence on the offence below. A score is roughly how many intended readers in ten would meet the problem at that sentence (0 = none, 9 = nearly all).

1. Height: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to feel at this sentence that the author, at the time of writing, does not command what they are telling: that they are finding it out as they write, guessing at it, or passing on what others know.

Spelling and grammar do not count.

Write a TSV and nothing else. One row per sentence where the score is 2 or more, in reading order: paragraph.sentence (e.g. 3.2), TAB, the score, TAB, why: in at most 15 words, what the reader meets at this sentence. Describe the stumble, not a way to fix it. Last line: END.

8.why: A twenty-year waller only "believes" the basic craft term is hearting.

9.why: The mechanism is guessed at: "presumably", "might"; not stated from experience.

10.why: Core technique is passed on from reading, "should probably", "I gather", "meant to".

11.why: Twenty years' practice ends in "could not say for certain why".
